body.heading: Watch the tempo
paragraphs: Every room has a tempo: fast and laughing, slow and heavy, brisk and businesslike. Matching your contribution to the tempo — not forcing a joke into a solemn moment, not dragging a celebration into a lecture — is most of what “reading the room” means.
If you are unsure of the tempo, enter quietly and let the room teach you. Thirty seconds of listening is rarely wasted.

body.heading: Notice who has gone quiet
paragraphs: Rooms change when someone stops participating. The person who was talking and now is not may be tired, hurt, or simply done — you cannot know which, but you can lower the cost of re-entry: a question tossed gently their way, or a topic change that gives them an easier door.
Do not announce it. “You’ve gone quiet” puts a spotlight where a lamp was needed.

body.heading: Let your read stay humble
paragraphs: Reading a room is guesswork, however skilled. Treat your conclusions as weather reports, not verdicts: useful for deciding whether to carry an umbrella, useless for judging the climate of a person’s whole life.
And when you misread — everyone does — a small, cheerful correction is enough. Rooms are forgiving to people who adjust quickly.

takeaway: Match the tempo, notice who has gone quiet, and hold your conclusions lightly.
